name: Adult polyglucosan body disease (GBE1)
aliases: glycogen branching enzyme deficiency, adult form

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents in mid-to-late adulthood with a triad of progressive spastic paraparesis, a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy and early neurogenic bladder dysfunction
Caused by deficiency of glycogen branching enzyme due to mutations in GBE1, leading to accumulation of poorly branched glycogen as polyglucosan bodies
Cognitive decline develops in a proportion of patients, adding a dementia component to the motor and bladder features
Early and prominent urinary symptoms out of proportion to the motor deficit are a useful clinical pointer
MRI often shows white matter change with involvement of the medulla and spinal cord and marked atrophy
Reduced branching enzyme activity in leucocytes or fibroblasts and characteristic polyglucosan bodies on nerve biopsy support the diagnosis
GBE1 genetic testing confirms the diagnosis, and the disorder is over-represented in people of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry
reference.pathophysiology: Adult polyglucosan body disease results from deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme encoded by GBE1, which normally introduces branch points into glycogen. Reduced enzyme activity leads to the synthesis of an abnormal, poorly branched, amylopectin-like glycogen that accumulates as intracellular polyglucosan bodies within neurones, glia and peripheral nerves, as well as other tissues. Deposition throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems produces axonal degeneration, demyelination and neuronal dysfunction, manifesting as the characteristic combination of spastic paraparesis, peripheral neuropathy, neurogenic bladder and, in some patients, cognitive impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and other motor neurone disorders
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and spinal cord to characterise white matter change and atrophy
Nerve conduction studies confirming a predominantly axonal peripheral neuropathy
Glycogen branching enzyme activity assay in leucocytes or cultured fibroblasts
GBE1 gene testing to confirm the diagnosis
Urodynamic assessment to characterise neurogenic bladder dysfunction
Nerve or other tissue biopsy demonstrating polyglucosan bodies when required
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness or bulbar involvement inconsistent with the expected slow course
Recurrent urinary retention or infection from an unrecognised neurogenic bladder
Falls and immobility from advancing spastic paraparesis
Cognitive decline raising safety and capacity concerns
reference.prognosis: The disorder progresses slowly over years, with accumulating gait impairment, bladder dysfunction and, in some, dementia leading to significant disability; management is supportive, targeting spasticity, bladder symptoms and mobility, and genetic counselling is offered.
pitfalls: Attributing early bladder symptoms to a urological cause and missing the underlying neurological disorder
Confusing the presentation with more common causes of spastic paraparesis without pursuing enzyme or genetic testing
Failing to consider the diagnosis in patients of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry with the characteristic triad
Overlooking peripheral neuropathy when spasticity dominates the clinical picture
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat spasticity with antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine alongside physiotherapy and stretching
Manage neurogenic bladder with anticholinergics, timed voiding and intermittent self-catheterisation, guided by urodynamic findings
Provide gait aids, orthoses, occupational therapy and falls prevention to preserve mobility
Manage the peripheral neuropathy symptomatically, including neuropathic pain agents and protective foot care
Support cognition and provide caregiver and psychological support where dementia develops
Monitor for complications such as recurrent urinary infection, pressure injury and swallowing difficulty over the progressive course
Offer genetic counselling and GBE1 carrier testing to at-risk relatives given autosomal recessive inheritance
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, urology, rehabilitation and specialist nursing
